currentKey: Increase the dose of fluticasone/salmeterol to twice daily.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
She is taking fluticasone/salmeterol **once daily**, but this product is labeled **twice daily** (COPD: 250/50 mcg, 1 inhalation BID). Correcting the regimen to its labeled frequency is the right first adjustment.
• **Salmeterol** is a 12-hour LABA, so once-daily use leaves her without bronchodilator or ICS coverage for half of each day. That fits her worsening dyspnea and frequent albuterol use.
• GOLD 2025 says to **check adherence, inhaler technique and correct use** before escalating or switching therapy. Using a BID product once daily is a use error that should be fixed first.
• This is **not ICS dose escalation**. In COPD, higher ICS doses add no benefit and raise pneumonia risk. The goal is labeled dosing of her current triple therapy (LAMA + LABA + ICS), which suits a patient with exacerbations requiring hospitalization.
• If she keeps exacerbating on correctly used triple therapy, GOLD's next options are **roflumilast** (FEV1 <50% with chronic bronchitis) or **azithromycin** (especially in former smokers). More ICS is not one of them.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Add a LABA**: She already takes salmeterol, a LABA. Adding a second LABA duplicates therapy and increases adverse effects (tachycardia, tremor, hypokalemia).
• **Switch from tiotropium to ipratropium**: Ipratropium is a short-acting muscarinic antagonist. Replacing a LAMA with it downgrades maintenance therapy, and a SAMA should not be combined with a LAMA.
• **Add a short course of oral corticosteroids**: Systemic steroids (for example prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days) treat an acute exacerbation. This question is about adjusting her maintenance regimen after hospitalization, and steroid bursts do not fix a dosing error.
## Key takeaway
Before escalating COPD therapy, confirm adherence, technique and correct dosing. Fluticasone/salmeterol is a twice-daily product. In COPD, ICS dose escalation is not the goal; if exacerbations continue on triple therapy, consider roflumilast or azithromycin.
(Guideline: GOLD 2025 report; fluticasone/salmeterol prescribing information)

currentKey: Advise increasing fruit and vegetable intake.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Advising more fruits and vegetables is the right *first* step, because her diet is clearly low in them and food-first counseling addresses the root problem.
• Fruits and vegetables supply folate, vitamin C, potassium and fiber. Vitamin C also improves absorption of dietary non-heme iron.
• **Fatigue in a menstruating woman should be evaluated**, not assumed to be dietary. Refer for a **CBC and ferritin** to check for iron-deficiency anemia before choosing an iron product.
• Because she could become pregnant (OCs can fail), USPSTF 2023 recommends **folic acid 0.4-0.8 mg daily** for anyone who is planning or capable of pregnancy. A multivitamin containing folic acid meets this.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Multivitamin with iron**: Iron is appropriate only once deficiency is confirmed. Starting it empirically can mask the workup and causes GI upset and constipation.
• **Vitamin D supplement**: Nothing in the case suggests vitamin D deficiency, and vitamin D does not treat fatigue.
• **Vitamin B12 information**: B12 deficiency is unlikely without risk factors (vegan diet, malabsorption, metformin or long-term acid suppression), so it is not the first step.
## Key takeaway
Start with diet, but evaluate fatigue (CBC or ferritin for iron deficiency) and recommend folic acid 0.4-0.8 mg daily for anyone who could become pregnant.
(Guideline: USPSTF 2023 folic acid recommendation; Dietary Guidelines for Americans 2020-2025)

currentKey: The patient's serum creatinine level is 2.5 mg/dL.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
An SCr of 2.5 mg/dL needs immediate follow-up because of what it means for his metformin.
• For a 60-year-old man, SCr 2.5 mg/dL gives an **eGFR of about 29 mL/min/1.73 m²** (CKD-EPI 2021), which is CKD stage G4.
• **Metformin is contraindicated at eGFR <30** (FDA 2016; KDIGO 2022) because it accumulates and raises the risk of lactic acidosis. Contact the prescriber to **stop metformin** and choose another agent (for example, a GLP-1 RA; SGLT2 inhibitors can be continued down to eGFR ≥20 for kidney protection).
• Review other renally cleared drugs and check **potassium** on lisinopril.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Taking atorvastatin**: Atorvastatin needs no renal dose adjustment and is appropriate (statins are recommended in CKD).
• **BP 140/90 mm Hg**: This is above goal (below 130/80; KDIGO suggests SBP <120 if tolerated) and should be addressed at follow-up, but it is not the urgent safety issue.
• **History of diabetes**: A chronic diagnosis, not a new finding that needs immediate action.
## Key takeaway
Always convert SCr to eGFR. An eGFR below 30 means stop metformin; at 30-44 the maximum is 1000 mg/day.
(Guideline: FDA metformin labeling 2016; KDIGO 2022 diabetes in CKD guideline)

currentKey: Verify the furosemide dose is appropriate for renal function.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Verifying the order is the first step before counseling or anything else. For furosemide at CrCl 40, "appropriate for renal function" means the dose may need to be **adequate or higher**, not lower.
• Furosemide must be secreted into the tubule to work. Reduced renal function means less drug reaches its site of action, so **patients with CKD often need higher loop diuretic doses** to get diuresis.
• It is **not dose-reduced** for CrCl 40. Confirm the dose matches the indication and volume status.
• Set up monitoring: **K⁺, Na⁺, Mg²⁺, SCr/BUN, BP, daily weight and symptoms of volume depletion**. Combining it with lisinopril raises the risk of hypotension and prerenal AKI.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Counsel on side effects**: Essential, but counseling comes after the order has been verified.
• **Check interactions with lisinopril and metoprolol**: Part of verification, but these are standard HF combinations (loop diuretic + ACE inhibitor + evidence-based beta-blocker) and not contraindications.
• **Contact prescriber about alternatives**: Nothing suggests furosemide is inappropriate for HF congestion.
## Key takeaway
Loop diuretics are not renally dose-reduced; CKD often needs higher doses. Verify the dose, then monitor electrolytes, renal function, BP and weight.
(Guideline: 2022 AHA/ACC/HFSA heart failure guideline; furosemide prescribing information)

## Why this answer is correct
Adding ezetimibe is guideline-concordant for this patient with clinical ASCVD whose LDL is far above threshold on a high-intensity statin.
• **Atorvastatin 40 mg is already high-intensity** (40-80 mg lowers LDL by ≥50%).
• In clinical ASCVD, add non-statin therapy when LDL stays **≥70 mg/dL** (≥55 mg/dL if very high risk, per the 2022 ACC ECDP) despite a maximally tolerated statin. There is no "<130" goal.
• **Ezetimibe** lowers LDL a further ~20-25%. Doubling the statin dose adds only ~6%, although atorvastatin 80 mg is also an acceptable step.
• An LDL of 160 on a high-intensity statin is striking. Confirm adherence, look for secondary causes (hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome) and consider **familial hypercholesterolemia**.
• Recheck a lipid panel in **4-12 weeks**. If LDL stays above threshold, a **PCSK9 monoclonal antibody** is the next step.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Increase atorvastatin to 80 mg**: Acceptable, but it adds only ~6% LDL lowering, far short of what he needs.
• **Switch to rosuvastatin 20 mg**: Another high-intensity statin at a roughly equivalent dose, so this is a lateral move.
• **Continue and recheck in 6 months**: Leaves a patient with clinical ASCVD at an LDL of 160 mg/dL for months without action.
## Key takeaway
Clinical ASCVD with LDL ≥70 (≥55 if very high risk) on a high-intensity statin: add ezetimibe, recheck in 4-12 weeks, then consider a PCSK9 mAb. An LDL of 160 on a high-intensity statin should prompt checking adherence and FH.
(Guideline: 2018 AHA/ACC cholesterol guideline; 2022 ACC ECDP on non-statin therapies)

currentKey: Remain upright for at least 30 minutes after taking alendronate.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Remaining upright for at least 30 minutes is the most important safety point for oral alendronate.
• Staying upright (sitting or standing) helps the tablet clear the esophagus and **prevents esophagitis, ulcers and erosions**, the main serious adverse effect.
• **Absorption** is a separate issue. Oral bioavailability is under 1%, so:
  • Take it first thing in the morning on an **empty stomach**.
  • Swallow it with **6-8 oz of plain water** only.
  • Wait **at least 30 minutes** before food, other drinks or other medicines, including calcium.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Take with food**: Food sharply reduces absorption and can make the drug ineffective.
• **Take at bedtime**: Lying down afterward raises esophageal injury risk, and the stomach is rarely empty at bedtime.
• **Take with milk**: Calcium in milk binds alendronate and blocks absorption. Use plain water only.
## Key takeaway
Alendronate: take in the morning on an empty stomach with plain water, stay upright ≥30 minutes (esophagus) and wait ≥30 minutes before food or other medicines (absorption).
(Guideline: Alendronate prescribing information; BHOF 2022 clinician's guide)

## Why this answer is correct
Doxylamine, used **together with pyridoxine (vitamin B6)**, is first-line drug therapy for nausea and vomiting of pregnancy.
• ACOG PB 189 recommends starting with **pyridoxine 10-25 mg alone** or **pyridoxine plus doxylamine**.
• Pyridoxine-doxylamine can be given as delayed-release 10 mg/10 mg (Diclegis) or 20 mg/20 mg (Bonjesta), or as OTC doxylamine 12.5 mg with pyridoxine 25 mg.
• It has the most reassuring fetal safety data of any NVP option.
• Nonpharmacologic measures (small frequent meals, ginger, avoiding triggers) should accompany it.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Ondansetron**: Reserved for symptoms not controlled by first-line therapy. Data on a small increase in oral clefts or cardiac defects are inconsistent, so it is not first-line.
• **Metoclopramide**: A later-line option (dopamine antagonist) with a risk of extrapyramidal effects. Not first-line.
• **Promethazine**: A second-line antihistamine/phenothiazine option when pyridoxine-doxylamine fails. Sedation limits it. It is not contraindicated in early pregnancy.
## Key takeaway
NVP first line is pyridoxine ± doxylamine. Next come antihistamines or dopamine antagonists (promethazine, metoclopramide), then ondansetron.
(Guideline: ACOG Practice Bulletin 189, 2018)

## Why this answer is correct
With SABA use more than twice a week and **nighttime symptoms**, her asthma is uncontrolled on SABA alone and she needs an **ICS-containing controller**. Fluticasone/salmeterol is the best option offered.
• Never manage asthma with SABA alone. The ICS treats airway inflammation and reduces exacerbations.
• **GINA preferred track:** low-dose **budesonide-formoterol** as maintenance-and-reliever (MART). NAEPP 2020 also prefers SMART at steps 3-4.
• **GINA alternative track:** maintenance **ICS-LABA** (such as fluticasone/salmeterol) with a SABA reliever. That is what this answer is.
• 250/50 mcg BID is a **medium ICS dose**. Once control is achieved, step down to the lowest effective dose.
• Check inhaler technique and adherence, and give a written action plan.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Montelukast**: Less effective than an ICS-containing controller. It also carries a boxed warning for neuropsychiatric events.
• **Budesonide as needed alone**: Without a scheduled controller or ICS-formoterol reliever this is not a standard regimen for her level of symptoms. Budesonide alone gives no bronchodilation.
• **Theophylline**: Narrow therapeutic index, many interactions, not recommended.
## Key takeaway
Uncontrolled asthma on SABA alone needs an ICS-containing controller. GINA prefers ICS-formoterol MART; ICS-LABA plus SABA is the alternative.
(Guideline: GINA 2024; NAEPP 2020 focused update)

currentKey: Take alendronate with a full glass of water and remain upright for 30 minutes.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Taking alendronate with a full glass of plain water (6-8 oz) and staying upright ≥30 minutes is the core counseling point. It reduces the risk of esophageal injury.
• Give it first thing in the morning on an empty stomach and wait ≥30 minutes before food, drinks or other medicines.
• **Her dysphagia and reflux history are red flags.** Oral bisphosphonates are **contraindicated** with esophageal abnormalities that delay emptying (stricture, achalasia) and in patients who cannot stay upright. They need **caution in active upper GI disease** (dysphagia, esophagitis).
• **Notify the prescriber.** Alternatives that avoid the esophagus include **IV zoledronic acid** (yearly) or **denosumab**.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Take at bedtime**: Lying down after the dose raises esophageal injury risk.
• **Take with food**: Food blocks absorption (bioavailability is already under 1%).
• **Avoid taking it when reflux flares**: Skipping doses based on symptoms is not a safe strategy. Symptoms of esophageal irritation (dysphagia, painful swallowing, heartburn) call for stopping and a prescriber evaluation.
## Key takeaway
Alendronate: plain water, empty stomach, upright ≥30 minutes. Dysphagia or esophageal disease means contacting the prescriber about IV zoledronic acid or denosumab.
(Guideline: Alendronate prescribing information; BHOF 2022; AACE 2020 osteoporosis guideline)

currentKey: Educate the patient on the importance of regular blood glucose monitoring.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Educating her on the purpose and use of glucose monitoring is a reasonable first step: identify the gap and explain why it matters before changing therapy.
• **ADA 2026:** On metformin without insulin or a sulfonylurea she has little hypoglycemia risk, so routine daily self-monitoring (SMBG) is **optional and individualized**. It is most useful when changing diet, activity or medications, during illness or with symptoms.
• Glycemic control is judged by **A1C every 3-6 months** (or CGM metrics when indicated).
• Education should cover when to check, target ranges (fasting 80-130 mg/dL) and how results guide care.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Increase metformin**: No glucose or A1C data justify a change. Metformin alone rarely causes hypoglycemia; the problem is changing a dose without data, not hypoglycemia risk.
• **Dietitian referral**: Medical nutrition therapy is valuable, but it does not address the gap identified in this session.
• **Review adherence**: Always part of MTM, but the finding in front of you is monitoring behavior, so address that first.
## Key takeaway
On metformin without insulin or a sulfonylurea, SMBG is individualized. Teach when monitoring helps, and use A1C (or CGM) to guide therapy.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026)

currentKey: Continue taking levothyroxine without any changes.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
She should continue levothyroxine as prescribed. It is the treatment of choice in pregnancy and should not be self-adjusted.
• Untreated or undertreated hypothyroidism raises the risk of miscarriage, preeclampsia, preterm birth and impaired fetal neurodevelopment.
• **Requirements rise about 20-30% in pregnancy.** Women already on levothyroxine typically increase the dose when pregnancy is confirmed (for example, two extra doses per week). The prescriber adjusts based on **TSH every 4 weeks through mid-gestation**, aiming for the lower half of the trimester-specific range (roughly <2.5 mIU/L).
• Take it on an empty stomach, 30-60 minutes before breakfast, and **separate prenatal vitamins (iron and calcium) by at least 4 hours**.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Reduce the dose**: Pregnancy needs go up, not down. Underdosing harms mother and fetus.
• **Switch thyroid medication**: Levothyroxine (T4) is preferred. T3-containing products (liothyronine, desiccated thyroid) do not reliably supply the T4 that crosses to the fetal brain.
• **Take with prenatal vitamins**: Iron and calcium bind levothyroxine and reduce absorption.
## Key takeaway
Continue levothyroxine in pregnancy. Expect a 20-30% dose increase, check TSH every 4 weeks in the first half and separate from iron or calcium by 4 hours.
(Guideline: 2017 ATA guideline for thyroid disease during pregnancy)

## Why this answer is correct
Budesonide/formoterol is the best option offered because it is the **only choice that adds a LABA** to his LAMA (tiotropium).
• **GOLD 2025:** Persistent dyspnea on LAMA monotherapy calls for **LAMA + LABA**, ideally in a single inhaler.
• An **ICS** is added (triple therapy) mainly for **exacerbations with blood eosinophils ≥300 cells/µL** (consider at ≥100 with exacerbations). ICS raises pneumonia risk, so it is not given for dyspnea alone.
• Budesonide/formoterol (160/4.5 mcg, 2 inhalations BID) is FDA-approved for COPD. Here the formoterol component drives the benefit. Check eosinophils and exacerbation history to decide whether the ICS is justified.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Montelukast**: No established role in COPD.
• **Theophylline**: Modest benefit, narrow therapeutic index, many interactions. Used only when long-acting bronchodilators are unavailable or unaffordable.
• **Ipratropium**: A short-acting antimuscarinic. It should not be added to a LAMA (duplicate anticholinergic effects) and does not give sustained bronchodilation.
## Key takeaway
COPD with dyspnea on a LAMA: add a LABA (LAMA/LABA). Add an ICS only for exacerbations with eosinophils ≥300 (or ≥100 with exacerbations).
(Guideline: GOLD 2025 report)

currentKey: Take metformin with food to minimize gastrointestinal side effects.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Taking metformin **with meals** is the most important counseling point. GI effects (nausea, diarrhea, abdominal discomfort) are the most common reason people stop it.
• Food and **slow titration** both reduce GI intolerance. The usual start is **500 mg once or twice daily**, increased by 500 mg weekly toward 1000 mg BID.
• Starting at 1000 mg BID is above the labeled starting dose. **Contact the prescriber** about a titration schedule; extended-release metformin is another option for GI intolerance.
• Her eGFR of 90 needs no adjustment. Recheck eGFR at least yearly, and periodically check **vitamin B12** with long-term use.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Monitor for hypoglycemia**: Metformin alone rarely causes hypoglycemia; the risk comes with insulin or sulfonylureas.
• **Stop metformin for any abdominal pain**: Mild GI upset is common and usually temporary. Severe abdominal pain with vomiting, malaise and rapid breathing needs urgent care (rare lactic acidosis), so counsel on those specific red flags instead.
• **Increase fluid intake**: Not a routine requirement. Do counsel her to hold metformin during dehydrating illness (vomiting, diarrhea).
## Key takeaway
Metformin: take with meals and start low (500 mg once or twice daily), titrating weekly. It rarely causes hypoglycemia alone.
(Guideline: Metformin prescribing information; ADA Standards of Care 2026)

## Why this answer is correct
Budesonide/formoterol is the best **maintenance** addition offered, because it is the only option that adds a **LABA** to his tiotropium.
• **GOLD 2025:** Persistent symptoms on a LAMA call for **LAMA + LABA**. An **ICS** is added mainly for exacerbations with blood eosinophils ≥300 cells/µL. Check eosinophils and exacerbation history to confirm whether the ICS component is warranted.
• **Clinical note:** A week of worsening dyspnea with more rescue use may be an **acute exacerbation**. If so, GOLD also recommends **prednisone 40 mg daily for 5 days** (plus antibiotics if sputum is purulent), alongside optimizing maintenance therapy.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Montelukast**: No established role in COPD.
• **Theophylline**: Narrow therapeutic index and many interactions. A last-line option.
• **Prednisone**: Treats an acute exacerbation for a short course only. It is not a maintenance drug, and long-term systemic steroids cause serious harm without benefit.
## Key takeaway
COPD on a LAMA with persistent dyspnea: add a LABA. Reserve ICS for exacerbations with eosinophilia. Treat an acute exacerbation with a 5-day steroid burst.
(Guideline: GOLD 2025 report)

currentKey: Take levothyroxine on an empty stomach, 30-60 minutes before other medications.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Levothyroxine should be taken **on an empty stomach** with water, **30-60 minutes before breakfast**. Absorption is best when fasting.
• **Calcium and iron** form complexes with levothyroxine and reduce absorption. Separate them by **at least 4 hours**, not just 30-60 minutes (for example, levothyroxine on waking and supplements with lunch or dinner).
• An alternative is bedtime dosing, at least 3 hours after the last meal.
• Consistency matters most: take it the same way every day so TSH-based dose adjustments stay reliable. Recheck TSH 6-8 weeks after any change in dose or supplements.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Take with calcium supplements**: Calcium binds levothyroxine and lowers absorption.
• **Take with iron supplements**: Iron also chelates levothyroxine. Separate by ≥4 hours.
• **Take with food**: Food (and coffee, soy, high fiber) reduces and varies absorption.
## Key takeaway
Levothyroxine: empty stomach, 30-60 minutes before breakfast, and at least 4 hours apart from calcium, iron and antacids.
(Guideline: ATA 2014 hypothyroidism treatment guideline; levothyroxine prescribing information)

currentKey: Limit sodium intake to help manage blood pressure.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Limiting sodium is the most appropriate dietary advice. It lowers BP and improves the response to antihypertensives.
• Aim for **<1500 mg sodium/day**, or at least a reduction of 1000 mg/day. DASH-style eating, weight loss, activity and limiting alcohol add to the effect.
• **Critical safety counseling:** ACE inhibitors carry a **boxed warning for fetal toxicity**. In a 30-year-old woman, confirm **effective contraception**, and tell her to stop the drug and contact the prescriber right away if she becomes pregnant.
• Also counsel on dry cough, dizziness with the first doses and **angioedema** (seek emergency care for lip, tongue or face swelling).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Avoid high-potassium foods**: With normal kidney function and no other potassium-raising drugs, dietary potassium is encouraged (it lowers BP). Advise her to avoid **potassium supplements and potassium-based salt substitutes** unless the prescriber approves.
• **Increase fluid intake**: Not required with lisinopril. Dehydration (vomiting, diarrhea) can cause hypotension or AKI, so counsel her to call if that happens.
• **Take at bedtime**: Lisinopril can be taken at any consistent time. Bedtime dosing does not reduce side effects.
## Key takeaway
With lisinopril, counsel sodium restriction and avoiding potassium supplements or salt substitutes. In women of childbearing potential, stress the fetal toxicity boxed warning and contraception.
(Guideline: 2025 AHA/ACC high blood pressure guideline; lisinopril prescribing information)

## Why this answer is correct
A 25(OH)D level of 25 ng/mL is below the **≥30 ng/mL target** used in osteoporosis care, so it calls for vitamin D supplementation.
• AACE 2020 and BHOF recommend keeping 25(OH)D **≥30 ng/mL** in patients with osteoporosis. Adequate vitamin D supports calcium absorption and the response to therapy, and **deficiency should be corrected before or with antiresorptive drugs** (it raises hypocalcemia risk).
• Typical correction: **vitamin D3 1000-2000 IU daily** (more if deficient), with total calcium intake of about 1200 mg/day from diet plus supplements.
• The 2024 Endocrine Society guideline sets no universal 25(OH)D threshold for the healthy general population. That does not replace osteoporosis-specific targets.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Calcium 9.0 mg/dL**: Normal (8.5-10.5). HCTZ can raise calcium slightly; monitor it but no change is needed.
• **SCr 0.9 mg/dL**: Normal renal function. Bisphosphonates are avoided only when CrCl is below 30-35 mL/min.
• **T-score -2.5**: This defines osteoporosis and is why therapy was started. It is the diagnosis, not a lab value that triggers a change.
## Key takeaway
In osteoporosis, keep 25(OH)D ≥30 ng/mL and correct deficiency before or with bisphosphonate therapy.
(Guideline: AACE/ACE 2020 postmenopausal osteoporosis guideline; BHOF 2022; Endocrine Society 2024 vitamin D guideline)

currentKey: Remain upright for at least 30 minutes after taking alendronate.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Staying upright for at least 30 minutes (with a full glass of plain water, on an empty stomach) is the key counseling point for preventing alendronate-related esophageal injury.
• **Her symptoms are a warning sign.** New **difficulty swallowing and abdominal pain** on a bisphosphonate may mean esophagitis or an ulcer. The label says to **stop the drug and seek evaluation** for dysphagia, painful swallowing, retrosternal pain or new or worsening heartburn.
• **Refer her to the prescriber now.** Parenteral options (IV zoledronic acid, denosumab) avoid the esophagus.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Take with food**: Food blocks absorption and does not prevent esophageal injury.
• **Increase calcium to 2000 mg daily**: Women over 50 need about **1200 mg/day total** (diet plus supplements). 2000 mg/day is the tolerable upper limit; more gives no benefit and raises kidney stone and GI risk.
• **Stop calcium supplements**: Calcium and vitamin D are needed with bisphosphonates. Take calcium at a different time of day (at least 30 minutes after alendronate; later in the day is simplest).
## Key takeaway
Alendronate means upright ≥30 minutes. New dysphagia or pain means stop and contact the prescriber. Keep calcium at about 1200 mg/day, separated from the dose.
(Guideline: Alendronate prescribing information; BHOF 2022; NAM dietary reference intakes)

## Why this answer is correct
Exenatide is the only **GLP-1 receptor agonist** among the options, so it matches the planned therapy.
• GLP-1 RAs increase glucose-dependent insulin secretion, lower glucagon, slow gastric emptying and promote weight loss, with low hypoglycemia risk on their own.
• **ADA 2026:** When intensifying therapy, **metformin is usually continued** (not replaced) unless it is contraindicated or not tolerated. Adding the GLP-1 RA to metformin is the usual approach.
• If he has ASCVD, ADA prefers a GLP-1 RA with **proven cardiovascular benefit** (semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide). Exenatide's CV outcome trial was neutral.
• Counsel on nausea (dose titration helps), pancreatitis symptoms and the thyroid C-cell tumor boxed warning for extended-release exenatide. Avoid exenatide when CrCl is below 30 mL/min.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Sitagliptin**: A DPP-4 inhibitor, not a GLP-1 RA. It should not be combined with a GLP-1 RA (overlapping mechanism, no added benefit).
• **Insulin glargine**: At A1C 8.5% without catabolic features, ADA prefers a GLP-1 RA before basal insulin. Insulin also adds weight gain and hypoglycemia risk.
• **Canagliflozin**: An SGLT2 inhibitor. Reasonable in general (especially with HF or CKD), but it is not the planned GLP-1 RA.
## Key takeaway
When adding a GLP-1 RA, keep metformin. Choose an agent with proven CV benefit if ASCVD is present. Never combine a GLP-1 RA with a DPP-4 inhibitor.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026)

currentKey: Monitor blood pressure regularly and report any significant changes.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Of the options, monitoring BP and reporting changes is best, but **her current symptomatic hypotension should be reported to the prescriber now**, not just watched.
• BP **90/60 mm Hg with lightheadedness** on lisinopril 20 mg suggests overtreatment or volume depletion. It raises the risk of falls, syncope and prerenal AKI.
• **Pharmacist action:** Contact the prescriber about **reducing or holding lisinopril**. Ask about vomiting, diarrhea, poor intake or new BP-lowering drugs, and check for orthostatic symptoms.
• Counsel her to rise slowly and to monitor home BP. During dehydrating illness, temporarily hold ACE inhibitors and metformin ("sick-day rules").
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Continue everything unchanged**: Ignores symptomatic hypotension and risks falls or AKI.
• **Increase fluid intake**: May help if she is volume-depleted, but it does not address overtreatment and is not a substitute for prescriber review.
• **Take metformin with food**: Good general advice, but it does not address the urgent problem.
## Key takeaway
Symptomatic hypotension on an antihypertensive means contacting the prescriber now for a dose change, then counseling on home BP monitoring and sick-day rules.
(Guideline: 2025 AHA/ACC high blood pressure guideline; lisinopril prescribing information)

## Why this answer is correct
Dapagliflozin is a guideline-supported addition. At A1C 8.5% on metformin plus a sulfonylurea, ADA 2026 favors an **SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 RA** because of low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk, weight benefit and cardiorenal protection.
• SGLT2 inhibitors lower A1C about 0.5-1% and reduce HF hospitalization and CKD progression.
• **Address the hypoglycemia:** he is already having lows on **glipizide**, and adding any glucose-lowering drug to a sulfonylurea increases that risk. **Recommend reducing or stopping glipizide** when dapagliflozin is started.
• Counsel on genital mycotic infections and hygiene, volume depletion (dizziness) and euglycemic DKA (hold at least 3 days before scheduled surgery and during acute illness).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Insulin glargine**: Not needed at A1C 8.5% without catabolic symptoms, and it would add hypoglycemia on top of glipizide.
• **Sitagliptin**: Modest A1C lowering, no cardiorenal benefit, and it increases hypoglycemia when combined with a sulfonylurea.
• **Pioglitazone**: Causes weight gain, edema and HF risk, plus fractures. It is not preferred over an SGLT2i when cardiorenal benefit is available.
## Key takeaway
When adding a drug to a sulfonylurea in someone with hypoglycemia, reduce or stop the sulfonylurea. SGLT2 inhibitors and GLP-1 RAs are preferred add-ons to metformin.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026)

## Why this answer is correct
Continuing metformin is the best of these options. Metformin remains foundational therapy for type 2 diabetes, and his CrCl of 70 mL/min allows full dosing.
• His **A1C of 8.2% is above the usual goal of <7%**. If he has already been taking metformin, continuing it is necessary but not sufficient: ADA 2026 recommends **timely intensification**, usually by **adding** a GLP-1 RA or SGLT2 inhibitor chosen by comorbidities (ASCVD, HF, CKD), weight goals and cost.
• If this is a **new** metformin start, monotherapy titrated from 500 mg with meals is reasonable at 8.2% (about 1.2% above goal); ADA considers early combination therapy when A1C is ≥1.5-2% above goal.
• Either way, metformin is continued, not replaced, when therapy is intensified, unless it is contraindicated or not tolerated. With his hypertension, a GLP-1 RA or SGLT2 inhibitor can also be considered for cardiorenal benefit.
• Recheck A1C in about 3 months, eGFR at least yearly and vitamin B12 periodically.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Start insulin immediately**: Insulin is favored first when A1C is >10%, glucose is ≥300 mg/dL or catabolic symptoms (weight loss, ketosis) are present. None apply here.
• **Increase atorvastatin**: Adults 40-75 with diabetes need at least a moderate-intensity statin (high-intensity with more risk factors), but no dose or lipid data are given, and this does not address glycemia.
• **Switch to a sulfonylurea**: Replacing metformin loses its benefits and adds hypoglycemia and weight gain. Sulfonylureas are not preferred add-ons when GLP-1 RAs or SGLT2 inhibitors are available.
## Key takeaway
Keep metformin as the foundation. An A1C above goal on metformin calls for adding a GLP-1 RA or SGLT2 inhibitor; insulin first is reserved for A1C >10%, glucose ≥300 or catabolic symptoms.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026)

## Why this answer is correct
Ezetimibe is the only appropriate **add-on** to atorvastatin among these options.
• Ezetimibe blocks intestinal cholesterol absorption (NPC1L1), lowering LDL a further ~20-25% on top of a statin with good tolerability.
• **First confirm statin intensity.** ACC/AHA 2018 recommends maximizing the statin to the intended intensity (for example atorvastatin 40-80 mg, high-intensity) before adding a non-statin. His atorvastatin dose is not stated. If he is on a moderate dose, uptitration is usually the first step.
• With LDL 160 mg/dL, also confirm adherence and look for secondary causes.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Simvastatin**: Adding a second statin to atorvastatin is **therapeutic duplication**. It raises myopathy risk without meaningful benefit.
• **Rosuvastatin**: Also duplicate statin therapy. Rosuvastatin could be used *instead of* atorvastatin, not with it.
• **Niacin**: Adding niacin to a statin did not reduce CV events (AIM-HIGH, HPS2-THRIVE) and increases flushing, hyperglycemia and hepatotoxicity. It is not recommended for LDL lowering.
## Key takeaway
Maximize statin intensity first; ezetimibe is the first-line non-statin add-on. Never combine two statins, and niacin has no outcome benefit.
(Guideline: 2018 AHA/ACC cholesterol guideline; 2022 ACC ECDP)

## Why this answer is correct
Ibuprofen with lisinopril is the only interaction among the options that involves **her actual medications**, so it poses the greatest risk.
• NSAIDs block renal prostaglandins. With an ACE inhibitor this **blunts the BP-lowering effect**, raises **potassium** and increases the risk of **acute kidney injury**. The risk is highest with dehydration, older age, CKD or a diuretic ("triple whammy").
• Ibuprofen 600 mg TID is also a problem because of her **peptic ulcer disease history**, a disease-drug concern. Prior PUD markedly raises NSAID ulcer and bleeding risk.
• **Recommendations:** For OA, prefer **topical NSAIDs** (knee or hand) or acetaminophen. If an oral NSAID is needed, use the lowest dose for the shortest time **with a PPI** (or consider a COX-2 inhibitor plus PPI). Monitor BP, SCr and K⁺.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Ibuprofen and aspirin**: A real interaction (more GI bleeding, less aspirin antiplatelet effect), but she is not taking aspirin.
• **Ibuprofen and warfarin**: A serious bleeding interaction, but she is not on warfarin.
• **Ibuprofen and acetaminophen**: No harmful interaction; they are often used together for pain.
## Key takeaway
NSAID plus ACE inhibitor means reduced BP control, hyperkalemia and AKI. With a history of PUD, avoid NSAIDs or add a PPI; for OA, prefer topical NSAIDs or acetaminophen.
(Guideline: ACG NSAID ulcer prevention guideline; 2019 ACR/AF osteoarthritis guideline; 2025 AHA/ACC high blood pressure guideline)

## Why this answer is correct
Adding a GLP-1 receptor agonist is the most appropriate step for A1C 8.5% on metformin.
• GLP-1 RAs lower A1C about 1-1.5%, cause meaningful weight loss and have low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk. Several (semaglutide, liraglutide, dulaglutide) have proven CV benefit.
• **Address his GI intolerance:** switch to **metformin extended-release** (better GI tolerance) rather than stopping metformin. GLP-1 RAs also cause nausea and diarrhea, so **start low and titrate slowly**, eat smaller meals and stop eating when full.
• Counsel on pancreatitis symptoms and the thyroid C-cell tumor boxed warning (avoid with personal or family history of MTC or MEN2).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Add a DPP-4 inhibitor**: Well tolerated but weaker (A1C about 0.5-0.8%), weight-neutral and without CV benefit.
• **Switch to insulin**: Not needed without A1C >10%, glucose ≥300 or catabolic features. It adds hypoglycemia and weight gain.
• **Increase metformin**: He is already at 2000 mg/day with GI intolerance. Higher doses add little glucose lowering and more GI effects.
## Key takeaway
For A1C above goal on metformin, add a GLP-1 RA. Manage GI effects by switching to metformin ER and titrating the GLP-1 RA slowly.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026)

## Why this answer is correct
Her asthma is uncontrolled on ICS-LABA (SABA use more than twice a week), so a step-up is indicated. Of the options, increasing the fluticasone/salmeterol dose is the appropriate one.
• **Before stepping up**, GINA requires checking **inhaler technique, adherence, triggers and comorbidities**. These are the most common causes of poor control.
• **GINA preferred step-up:** switch to **budesonide-formoterol maintenance-and-reliever therapy (MART)**, which reduces severe exacerbations compared with a higher fixed ICS-LABA dose plus SABA. **Alternative track:** increase to a higher ICS-LABA dose (this answer) with a SABA reliever.
• Reassess control in 2-3 months and step down once stable.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Continue and monitor**: She is uncontrolled, and doing nothing leaves her at risk of exacerbations.
• **Add a LABA**: She already gets a LABA (salmeterol) in her combination inhaler. Adding another duplicates therapy.
• **Refer to a specialist**: Appropriate for step 5, severe or difficult-to-treat asthma, or diagnostic doubt. It is not the first step for SABA use slightly above twice a week.
## Key takeaway
Uncontrolled asthma means check technique and adherence, then step up: ICS-formoterol MART is preferred, and a higher-dose ICS-LABA is the alternative.
(Guideline: GINA 2024; NAEPP 2020 focused update)

## Why this answer is correct
New **increased thirst and urination** over weeks is a symptom of **uncontrolled hyperglycemia** (osmotic diuresis) and needs prompt evaluation.
• Check blood glucose and A1C now. Marked hyperglycemia with polyuria and dehydration can progress to **hyperosmolar hyperglycemic state** in T2D, and dehydration can also worsen his kidney function.
• **Medication review at eGFR 35:** metformin is **limited to ≤1000 mg/day at eGFR 30-44** (stop below 30). Monitor eGFR every 3-6 months.
• For intensification in T2D with CKD, consider a **GLP-1 RA** for glucose lowering and an **SGLT2 inhibitor** (eGFR ≥20) for kidney and heart protection. Continue the ACE inhibitor and monitor K⁺.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **SCr 2.1 mg/dL**: Consistent with his known CKD. It needs dose review but is not a new acute change.
• **Metformin and lisinopril**: Both are appropriate in diabetic CKD, provided metformin is dose-limited for eGFR 35.
• **eGFR 35**: Describes chronic stage G3b disease. It drives dosing decisions but is not the new, symptomatic finding.
## Key takeaway
New polyuria and polydipsia in diabetes means checking glucose and evaluating for hyperglycemia. At eGFR 30-44, cap metformin at 1000 mg/day.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care 2026; KDIGO 2022; FDA metformin labeling 2016)

## Why this answer is correct
Ezetimibe 10 mg daily is the best **add-on** for further LDL lowering.
• **Atorvastatin 40 mg is already high-intensity** (≥50% LDL reduction expected). When LDL stays high on a high-intensity statin, **ezetimibe is the first non-statin add-on**, giving about 20-25% more LDL lowering with good tolerability.
• An LDL of 160 on atorvastatin 40 mg is unexpectedly high. **Confirm adherence**, look for secondary causes (hypothyroidism, nephrotic syndrome, cholestasis) and consider familial hypercholesterolemia.
• Recheck the lipid panel 4-12 weeks after the change. If LDL remains above threshold in high-risk patients, a PCSK9 mAb is next.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Fenofibrate**: Mainly lowers triglycerides, with minimal LDL effect. Adding it to a statin has not reduced CV events.
• **Niacin**: No CV benefit when added to statins (AIM-HIGH, HPS2-THRIVE), with flushing, hyperglycemia and hepatotoxicity.
• **Rosuvastatin 20 mg**: Roughly equipotent to atorvastatin 40 mg. Switching is lateral, and adding it would be duplicate statin therapy.
## Key takeaway
LDL above threshold on a high-intensity statin: confirm adherence, then add ezetimibe as the first non-statin agent.
(Guideline: 2018 AHA/ACC cholesterol guideline; 2022 ACC ECDP)

## Why this answer is correct
An SGLT2 inhibitor is a guideline-preferred add-on to metformin. It has low intrinsic hypoglycemia risk, causes modest weight loss and provides heart failure and CKD benefit.
• **His hypoglycemia comes from glipizide.** Adding any glucose-lowering agent to a sulfonylurea can worsen lows, so **reduce or stop glipizide** when the SGLT2 inhibitor starts.
• A GLP-1 RA would be an equally guideline-supported choice (not offered).
• Counsel on genital mycotic infections, volume depletion and euglycemic DKA (hold before surgery and during acute illness).
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Insulin glargine**: Not needed at A1C 8.5% without catabolic features, and it would add to the hypoglycemia.
• **DPP-4 inhibitor**: Modest efficacy and no cardiorenal benefit. It also raises hypoglycemia risk when combined with a sulfonylurea.
• **Sulfonylurea**: He is already on one (glipizide). Adding another is duplication and would worsen hypoglycemia.
## Key takeaway
When a patient on a sulfonylurea has hypoglycemia and needs intensification, add an SGLT2i or GLP-1 RA and reduce or stop the sulfonylurea.
(Guideline: ADA Standards of Care in Diabetes 2026)

currentKey: Contact the prescriber for possible medication adjustment.
explanation:
## Why this answer is correct
Rising albuterol use on a controller regimen (fluticasone plus montelukast) means her **asthma is not controlled**, so the prescriber needs to reassess and probably step up therapy.
• **Technique and adherence are not secondary.** GINA says to check inhaler technique, adherence, trigger exposure and comorbidities **before any step-up**, since these explain most poor control. A pharmacist can do this during the same encounter and include the findings when contacting the prescriber.
• Likely step-up options: switch to **ICS-formoterol maintenance-and-reliever therapy** (GINA preferred) or to ICS-LABA. Montelukast adds little and carries a neuropsychiatric boxed warning.
• Make sure she has an up-to-date written asthma action plan.
## Why the other options are wrong
• **Counsel on inhaler technique**: Essential, and GINA recommends it before stepping up, but technique counseling alone does not resolve worsening control. The prescriber still needs to reassess the regimen. (Ideally do both.)
• **Increase albuterol use**: Relying more on SABA signals and worsens poor control. SABA overuse is linked to exacerbations and asthma deaths.
• **Monitor peak flow**: Useful for self-management, but it does not act on the deterioration already present.
## Key takeaway
Rising SABA use on controllers means poor control. Check technique and adherence, and contact the prescriber for a step-up (ICS-formoterol MART preferred).
(Guideline: GINA 2024)
